title: Advanced Database Internals
description: Advanced Database Internals. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Explain MVCC snapshots and why updates create new row versions in PostgreSQL.
Diagnose vacuum pressure, dead tuples, bloat, and transaction-ID wraparound risk.
Trace how WAL, checkpoints, and crash recovery support durability.
Reason about locks, blocking, deadlocks, and transaction isolation.

mentalModel.text: A database has to let many people read and change data at once, recover after a crash, and clean up old data safely. PostgreSQL tracks row versions, records changes for recovery, and uses locks to coordinate conflicting work. Many production problems happen when a long transaction or busy workload stops these systems from keeping up.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL uses multi-version concurrency control (MVCC): when a transaction updates a row, it usually creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one immediately. A query sees the version allowed by its snapshot. This lets readers and writers work at the same time, but old versions cannot be cleaned up while an active transaction might still need them.

blocks.title: Find long transactions
blocks.source:
SELECT pid, xact_start, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY xact_start;

blocks.problem: A report transaction has been open for 45 minutes while a high-write table accumulates dead tuples.
reasoning: Check transaction age and isolation level; determine whether its snapshot prevents cleanup of versions it might still need.
Compare dead-tuple estimates, autovacuum activity, table size, and write rate.
Fix the transaction lifecycle or workload, then verify vacuum can make progress.
blocks.outcome: MVCC improves concurrency but makes transaction duration and cleanup progress operational concerns.

blocks.text: Updates and deletes can leave old row versions behind. VACUUM cleans up versions that no active transaction needs and makes their space reusable. Regular VACUUM usually does not shrink the file on disk; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and needs a stronger lock, so it is a more disruptive fix.

blocks.title: Inspect vacuum statistics

blocks.problem: Dead tuples rise for hours and autovacuum cannot catch up.
reasoning: Compare tuple generation with vacuum throughput and inspect long transactions, replication slots, and vacuum logs.
Check thresholds, cost limits, table-specific settings, and resource contention.
Address the blocker or throughput gap before planning a disruptive rewrite.
blocks.outcome: Bloat is often a symptom of cleanup falling behind or being blocked. Diagnose why cleanup cannot keep pace.

blocks.text: Before PostgreSQL relies on a changed data page being written to disk, it records the change in the write-ahead log (WAL). After a crash, it can replay the saved log to recover changes. Checkpoints limit how much log must be replayed, but heavy checkpoints can cause bursts of disk activity.

blocks.title: Inspect checkpoint signals
blocks.source:
SELECT checkpoints_timed, checkpoints_req, checkpoint_write_time, checkpoint_sync_time, buffers_checkpoint, buffers_backend
FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;

blocks.title: Interpret signals
rows: WAL volume or settings may force checkpoints

blocks.text: A query is blocked when it needs something another transaction holds. A deadlock happens when transactions wait on each other in a cycle: A holds one row and waits for another, while B holds the second and waits for the first. PostgreSQL aborts one transaction so the other can continue.

blocks.title: Find blocked sessions

blocks.problem: Two workers update the same pair of accounts in opposite order.
reasoning: Identify the cycle: one worker holds X and waits for Y while the other holds Y and waits for X.
Acquire rows in a consistent order, such as ascending account ID.
Retry the complete transaction safely when a deadlock victim is aborted.
blocks.outcome: Consistent lock ordering reduces deadlocks; short transactions and safe retries improve resilience.

blocks.text: Isolation levels control what a transaction can see while others change data. READ COMMITTED gets a fresh view for each statement; REPEATABLE READ keeps a stable view for the transaction; SERIALIZABLE can reject a transaction if its result would not fit a safe serial order. The application must handle those retries.

blocks.title: Atomic conditional update
Isolation choice
rows: Multi-statement invariants need constraints or locks

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Avoid symptom-only fixes
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Identify the mechanism and validate it with workload evidence before changing database settings.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Answer like an engineer
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: State the invariant, explain the failure mode, propose a measurable intervention, and describe a safety or rollback check.

revisionSheet.text: MVCC snapshots determine visibility; long transactions can delay cleanup.
Standard VACUUM makes space reusable; VACUUM FULL rewrites and locks more strongly.
WAL supports crash recovery; checkpoint behavior influences write I/O.
Use lock graphs, consistent lock order, constraints, and safe transaction retries.

questions.prompt: Two transactions read a row while one updates it. What lets the reader retain a consistent view?

options.text: Snapshot and tuple-visibility rules
A global pause on all writes
Immediate overwrite of every old version
An exclusive table lock for every SELECT

questions.explanation: MVCC snapshots determine which tuple versions are visible.

questions.prompt: Dead tuples rise while a transaction remains open for 50 minutes. What should you investigate first?

options.text: Whether the long transaction or another retained snapshot blocks cleanup
Run VACUUM FULL on every table immediately
Increase shared_buffers without checking activity
Drop all indexes

questions.explanation: Long-lived snapshots can prevent removal of row versions still potentially visible.

questions.prompt: What does standard VACUUM usually do with dead-tuple space?

options.text: Makes eligible space reusable within the relation
Always returns all free space to the OS
Rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock
Deletes WAL needed by replicas

questions.explanation: Standard VACUUM generally makes space reusable; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table.

questions.prompt: Why record WAL before relying on modified data pages being persisted?

options.text: Crash recovery can replay durable changes
WAL eliminates checkpoints
WAL makes every query faster
WAL replaces indexes

questions.explanation: WAL supports recovery by recording changes before affected data pages must be flushed.

questions.prompt: A lock blocker is idle in transaction. What is the main concern?

options.text: It may retain locks or an old snapshot while doing no useful work
The database has no lock manager
The blocked query must lack an index
The server has automatically rolled back the blocker

questions.explanation: An idle open transaction can retain locks and snapshots; inspect impact before terminating it.

questions.prompt: Two transfer code paths update accounts in opposite order and deadlock. What design change helps most?

options.text: Acquire rows in consistent order and retry safe deadlock victims
Disable deadlock detection
Use SERIALIZABLE without retries
Add an index and assume the cycle disappears

questions.explanation: Consistent lock ordering breaks this common cycle; retry handling is still needed.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, how do snapshots normally behave?

options.text: Each statement sees a new snapshot
All statements share one transaction-wide snapshot
Reads see other transactions' uncommitted writes
All serialization anomalies are prevented

questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED uses a new snapshot for each statement.

questions.prompt: An application uses SERIALIZABLE to protect a critical invariant. What must it plan for?

options.text: Serialization failures and safe transaction retries
A guarantee that no transaction will abort
Lock-free execution for all statements
Removal of all constraints

questions.explanation: Serializable semantics may require aborting transactions that cannot be serialized safely.

questions.prompt: Which conditions can delay cleanup of old tuple versions?

options.text: Long-running transaction with old snapshot
Replication slot retaining required history/WAL
Standby feedback holding back cleanup
A finished SELECT whose snapshot has been released

questions.explanation: Long snapshots and replication-related retention can delay cleanup; completed statements no longer retain their snapshot.

questions.prompt: Which signals help diagnose checkpoint-related write spikes?

options.text: Requested versus timed checkpoints
Checkpoint write/sync time and dirty buffers
WAL generation and storage latency
Number of SQL keywords in the query

questions.explanation: Checkpoint counts, timing, WAL volume, and storage behavior help identify pressure.

questions.prompt: Standard VACUUM always returns all reclaimable table space to the operating system.
questions.explanation: Standard VACUUM normally makes space reusable within the relation.

questions.prompt: A deadlock victim's transaction is aborted, so application code must not assume its writes committed.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL aborts one participant in a deadlock cycle.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A high-write table is growing rapidly, autovacuum runs constantly, and a long report transaction is open.
strongAnswerPoints: Check transaction age and retained snapshots.
Inspect replication slots, vacuum progress, and write rate.
Resolve the blocker before considering a disruptive rewrite.
pitfalls: Treating VACUUM FULL as the default fix
Changing several variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would determine why old versions cannot be removed, starting with long transactions and replication retention. Then I would compare dead-tuple generation with vacuum throughput, resolve the blocker, and verify cleanup catches up before considering a rewrite.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A service sees latency spikes and deadlocks during account transfers. What changes would you make?
strongAnswerPoints: Use blocking/deadlock logs to identify the cycle.
Standardize lock order and use atomic updates.
Add bounded retry for safe transaction aborts.
pitfalls: Retrying only part of an aborted transaction
Changing several variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would identify the wait cycle, standardize lock ordering, keep transactions short, and retry the whole transaction on a known abort. I would add concurrency tests to verify balances remain correct.
